Ngữ pháp: trộn câu đơn – câu phức tự nhiên; đa dạng thì và cấu trúc (used to, I'd say, from my own experience…) mà vẫn rất ít lỗi.
Phát âm: rõ ràng, đúng trọng âm từ và câu, ngữ điệu lên xuống thể hiện thái độ; nối âm tự nhiên; giữ âm cuối (-s, -ed, -t) – lỗi người Việt hay gặp nhất.

sections.intro: Có 1 phút chuẩn bị (được ghi chú) rồi nói liên tục 1–2 phút. Giám khảo sẽ dừng bạn khi hết 2 phút – nên nhắm nói đủ khoảng 1 phút 45 giây trở lên.

tasks.p:
Describe an old object that your family has kept for a long time.
You should say:
• what the object is
• where it came from
• how it has been kept or used over the years
and explain why it is important to your family.
tasks.model:
The object I'd like to talk about is a hand-operated sewing machine that originally belonged to my great-grandmother, and which now sits in a corner of my parents' living room.

As far as we know, she bought it second-hand in the late nineteen-fifties, in the market town near her village. It must have cost her a small fortune at the time, because the family story is that she saved for almost two years, selling vegetables and eggs, before she could afford it. It's made of black cast iron with faded gold patterns on the side, and it still has its original wooden cover, although most of the varnish has worn away.

For decades, that machine was genuinely essential. My great-grandmother made clothes for the whole family on it, and later she took in sewing work from the neighbours, which helped pay for my grandfather's schooling. When she passed away, it went to my grandmother, who used it right up until the early two-thousands, mainly for mending. Nowadays nobody actually sews with it, but my father oils it every year or so, and remarkably, it still works perfectly.

As for why it matters so much, I think it's because it represents a kind of quiet determination that we're all rather proud of. It's a reminder that the comfortable life we have today was built by people who worked incredibly hard with very little. My mother sometimes says it's the most valuable thing in the house, even though it would probably fetch very little if we ever sold it. And I suspect that one day, when it's passed on to me, I'll feel exactly the same way.
tips: Dùng 1 phút ghi 4–5 từ khoá theo 4 gạch đầu dòng, không viết câu hoàn chỉnh.
Thêm chi tiết cụ thể (năm, nơi, câu chuyện gia đình) để nói đủ 2 phút một cách tự nhiên.
Phần ‘explain why’ là nơi thể hiện từ vựng trừu tượng (determination, a reminder that…) – để dành ít nhất 30 giây.

rubric: Độ trôi chảy & mạch lạc: nói liên tục đủ thời gian, đi lần lượt các gợi ý trên thẻ, có mở – thân – kết rõ ràng; chuyển ý mượt (As far as we know, As for why…).
Vốn từ: mô tả vật cụ thể (cast iron, varnish, second-hand) và cảm xúc, giá trị trừu tượng (quiet determination, a reminder that…) chính xác.
Ngữ pháp: dùng tự nhiên các thì quá khứ, hiện tại hoàn thành, động từ khuyết thiếu suy đoán (must have cost), mệnh đề quan hệ, bị động (when it's passed on to me).
Phát âm: nhấn mạnh từ mang ý chính, ngắt nhịp theo cụm ý, không đọc đều đều như học thuộc.

sections.intro: Khoảng 4–5 phút. Câu hỏi trừu tượng mở rộng từ chủ đề Part 2 (di sản, quá khứ, bảo tồn). Trả lời 4–6 câu: nêu quan điểm → lý do → ví dụ/so sánh → nhượng bộ hoặc kết luận.

tasks.p: Why do you think some people enjoy collecting old things?
tasks.model: I think there are several motivations. For some people it's essentially about connection with the past: holding a coin or a letter that's a hundred years old gives you a tangible link to people who lived very different lives. For others it's more about the thrill of the hunt, searching flea markets or online auctions for the one missing piece. And there's an investment side too, since certain antiques increase in value. Personally, I suspect the deepest reason is that old objects carry stories, and in a world where so much is mass-produced and disposable, owning something with a history feels quite meaningful.

tasks.p: Should governments spend money on preserving old buildings, or would it be better to build new ones?
tasks.model: It depends on the building, but generally I'd argue that preservation deserves public funding. Historic buildings give a city its character, and once they've been demolished, they can never be replaced. They also tend to attract tourism, which brings economic benefits. That said, I don't think every old structure should be protected at any cost; in fast-growing cities where housing is desperately needed, there has to be a balance. One sensible compromise is adaptive reuse – turning an old factory into flats, say, or a former market into a cultural centre – which keeps the heritage while meeting modern needs.

tasks.p: How has technology changed the way people learn about history?
tasks.model: Quite dramatically, I'd say. A generation ago, most people encountered history through textbooks, which could be rather dry. Now there's an enormous range of options: documentaries, podcasts, virtual museum tours, even apps that let you point your phone at a ruin and see a reconstruction of how it once looked. On the positive side, this makes history far more accessible and engaging, especially for young people. The downside is that there's also a great deal of inaccurate or sensationalised content online, so people need to be much more critical of their sources than they used to be.

tasks.p: Do you think museums will still be important in the future?
tasks.model: I believe so, although their role will probably evolve. It's true that you can now view high-resolution images of almost any famous artwork online, but I don't think that replaces the experience of standing in front of the real thing; there's an authenticity to it that a screen simply can't reproduce. I imagine future museums will become more interactive and more like community spaces, hosting workshops and debates rather than just displaying objects behind glass. If they adapt in that way, I think they'll remain highly relevant.

tasks.p: Who should decide which objects or places are worth preserving: experts or ordinary people?
tasks.model: Ideally, both should have a say. Experts obviously bring essential knowledge: an archaeologist can recognise the significance of something that might look like a pile of old stones to the rest of us. But if decisions are left entirely to specialists, there's a risk of overlooking what matters to local communities, such as a modest temple or an old market that has deep emotional value but little architectural merit. So I think the best approach is for experts to provide the evidence and advice, while residents are genuinely consulted, perhaps through public meetings, before any final decision is made.

rubric: Độ trôi chảy & mạch lạc: phát triển ý dài, có lập luận nhiều tầng (một mặt – mặt khác – kết luận); không trả lời cụt hoặc lặp lại câu hỏi.
Vốn từ: dùng từ trừu tượng, học thuật đúng chỗ (tangible link, adaptive reuse, authenticity, sensationalised, architectural merit) và cụm nhượng bộ (That said, It's true that… but…).

sections.h: Listening – Part 1 · Booking a beginner workshop
sections.intro: Questions 1–10: hoàn thành mẫu đặt chỗ. Theo giới hạn từ/số trong mỗi câu. Các chi phí và đặt chỗ đều là dữ liệu giả cho bài luyện.

dialog.note: Nghe cuộc trao đổi để ghi thông tin đặt chỗ được chốt, chú ý số hoặc ngày đã sửa và cách đánh vần.

lines.t: Hello, I’m calling about the introductory bookbinding workshop at your fictional Leravin Craft House. I saw a notice for a Friday evening session, but our group cannot come then. Is there another session for beginners?

Yes. That notice was for last month. The next beginner workshop is on Saturday. We keep the evening sessions for people who have already attended an introduction, because the tutor moves more quickly and does not repeat the equipment demonstration.
Saturday would suit us. My surname is Velmora. I’ll spell that because it is sometimes written with an extra letter: V, E, L, M, O, R, A. I’m making the booking for the group, but I’m not a tutor.

Thank you. We only need one booking contact. You can give the other first names when you arrive. How many places would you like me to reserve? The notice says groups can book up to six, although smaller groups are welcome too.

There were going to be six of us, but two friends have other plans now. Please reserve four places. We don’t want to keep places that somebody else could use. Is there a minimum age for the beginner activity?

The activity on this booking is for adults. We have a separate family session with a different pace. Your group of four can join the main introduction. It begins at ten thirty, not ten. Please arrive about fifteen minutes earlier so we can show everyone where to leave bags.

That is clear. One person read ten on the old notice, so I’ll correct our message. Which room should we ask for? Last time I visited the house, the reception team sent everyone upstairs because the ground floor was being painted.

The painting is finished. You will use the ground-floor room called Nerafin. It is the first room beyond reception, but don’t join the queue outside the music room. That queue belongs to a different activity starting at the same time.
What is the fee for this beginner session? We have our own paper, and I wondered whether bringing it would change the cost. I don’t want to assume that materials are included if they aren’t.

The fee is eighteen pounds per person in this invented booking. Basic paper is included. We do not reduce the fee for personal materials because the main costs are teaching and equipment. You can bring your paper to ask about it, but the first practice book uses ours.
Fine. Should we bring gloves or anything to protect our clothes? The notice has a photograph of somebody wearing an apron, but it does not list what visitors need to provide themselves.

Please bring an apron. We provide the small tools and explain their use before the activity. The photograph also shows a storage cover on the table; that is not something you need to bring. A notebook is optional if you like writing reminders.
One person in our group would prefer an entrance without steps. Is there a way to reach the room on the ground floor without using the two steps by the front sign?

Yes, use the ramp beside the courtyard. Follow the same covered path from there to reception. Please don’t use the delivery door at the back, even if it is open. Staff moving boxes need to keep that route clear.
I’ll pass that on. What do you need from me before Saturday? I can collect names now, but I don’t yet know whether everyone wants to keep the book or give it to somebody afterwards.

We don’t need to know what they will do with it. Please return the confirmation form by Thursday. The earlier reminder said Wednesday, but we extended it so the tutor can finalise groups on Friday morning.
And where do I pick up the form? I can visit tomorrow if there is a printed copy. It would be helpful to see the room location before the group arrives on Saturday.
Collect it from the entrance desk. The workshop tutor is not there every day, so please don’t wait outside the room for a form. The entrance team can mark your reservation and show you the route.
Thank you. I have Saturday at ten thirty, four places, the Nerafin room and eighteen pounds each. We’ll bring aprons, use the ramp if needed and return the form by Thursday.
Exactly. Those are the confirmed details. If your group changes, please tell the entrance team rather than booking a second group under the same name. That helps us keep the place count accurate.

items.e: Apron cần tự mang; tools do trung tâm cấp, notebook tùy chọn.

sections.intro: Questions 11–20: nghe hướng dẫn. Câu trắc nghiệm chọn một phương án; câu điền theo giới hạn ghi riêng. Các phòng và hoạt động đều hư cấu.

dialog.note: Nghe hướng dẫn đường đi và hoạt động, tách nơi có thể ghé tự do với phòng cần đặt trước.

lines.t: Welcome to the fictional Orelan Sound and Story Centre. I’m Mela, one of the volunteers showing new visitors around. The building was once a storage house, but our purpose is not to tell the history of storage. We provide a place where people can make and share original accounts of everyday life. You do not need a remarkable family collection or a dramatic event to take part. A careful description of an ordinary place can be just as interesting.

Before we begin, notice the coloured patterns on the floor. Some visitors think they were added to make the building look older. In fact, we kept them because they help people recognise which part of the house they are in. The green strip leads towards the courtyard; the blue strip ends outside the recording rooms. You can ask a volunteer for directions, but the strips remain useful when the desk is busy.

The Blue Room is not a general quiet room, although it has the thickest door. It is reserved for booked recordings. Please do not open it simply to look inside, because that can interrupt a speaker halfway through an account. There is a small window beside the door where a sign shows whether a session is in progress. Anyone wanting to make a first recording should arrange an introduction at reception rather than wait here for an empty moment.

If you want somewhere to read without recording, use the room to the left of the courtyard. It has ordinary chairs and a short selection of practice texts written for the centre. The room on the right contains an exhibition of draft scripts, so groups sometimes discuss work there. Both are useful, but they do not provide the same kind of quiet. The reading room has no reservation list; if every seat is occupied, please ask at the desk about another suitable space.

Our Saturday introductory talk has moved. It used to begin at ten fifteen, and an old leaflet gives eleven. Neither is the current time. The talk now begins at ten forty-five so that people arriving for the morning activities can hear it before they divide into groups. You do not need a separate ticket. We ask only that you arrive before the first recording example, because a late entrance makes it harder for others to follow.

Headphones can be borrowed from the reception desk. They are not kept in the recording rooms, and the exhibition shop does not lend equipment. Please return them to the same desk rather than leave them on a chair. You can listen at the demonstration station without signing up for a recording workshop. The station plays accounts created specifically for this fictional centre, not private recordings left by previous visitors.

We are also inviting new volunteers. Previous experience with recording equipment is welcome but not required. Everyone first observes a session and receives guidance about the particular task they will do. Please do not promise to operate a recorder alone just because you have used a similar device elsewhere. Helping visitors find a room or understand a label is equally valuable work. The sign-up card asks about the time you can offer, not a list of impressive equipment names.

Some visitors would like an object or photograph included in a future display. We do not ask you to leave the original today. Complete an interest form and describe what you have in mind. A photograph can help us understand its size and appearance, but it is not a requirement for this first conversation. We will discuss the story, the proposed display and permission before arranging any loan.

You are welcome to eat your own lunch in the courtyard. Food is not sold here today, and the exhibition tables are not lunch tables. The covered part of the courtyard can still be used if there is light rain. Please keep the central route clear, since people use it to move between the reading room and reception. There is no need to hurry through lunch in order to attend a workshop; the afternoon sessions start separately.

Finally, we would like feedback from people who tried an activity and those who only looked around. At the exit, you will find a short card asking what you could do here and what remained unclear. We are not asking for a rating of the staff member who greeted you. A specific comment about a room, a sign or an activity will help us decide what to explain better. Thank you; we’ll now follow the green strip towards the courtyard.

items.q: 11. What is the centre’s main purpose?
o: To collect dramatic family events exclusively
To help people create and share original everyday accounts
items.e: Người nói nêu make and share original accounts of everyday life; không giới hạn sự kiện kịch tính.

items.q: 12. Why were the floor patterns retained?
o: They help visitors identify different areas
They prove the building is ancient
items.e: Patterns được giữ vì định hướng; ý trang trí cho trông cũ bị bác.

items.q: 13. What is the Blue Room used for?
items.e: Thick door không khiến nó thành general quiet room; booked recordings là chức năng.

items.q: 14. Which room provides unbooked quiet reading?
o: The Blue Room during any empty moment
The room left of the courtyard
The exhibition room on the right
items.e: Room left có chairs và practice texts, không reservation list.

items.q: 15. Current Saturday talk time: ___ (A NUMBER)
items.e: Ten fifteen là giờ trước, eleven trong leaflet cũ; ten forty-five là hiện tại.

items.q: 16. Headphones are borrowed from the ___ desk. (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: Reception desk vừa cho mượn vừa nhận trả; shop không lend equipment.

items.q: 17. What is said about new volunteers?
o: They should promise to operate equipment alone
They receive guidance before their assigned task
All must already be recording experts
items.e: Previous experience không bắt buộc; quan sát và guidance đi trước công việc.

items.q: 18. To suggest an item for display, complete an ___ form. (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: Không cần để original ngay hoặc phải có ảnh; bước đầu là interest form.

items.q: 19. Visitors may eat their own lunch in the ___ (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: Courtyard là chỗ ăn, không exhibition tables; hôm đó không bán đồ ăn.

items.q: 20. What feedback is requested?
o: Specific comments about what visitors could do or did not understand
Only a rating of the person at reception
items.e: Mời cả người chỉ tham quan, muốn nhận xét room/sign/activity thay chấm người chào.

sections.h: Listening – Part 3 · Planning a seating investigation
sections.intro: Questions 21–30: chọn một đáp án đúng cho mỗi câu. Hai sinh viên đang lập kế hoạch bài tập thiết kế hư cấu; theo các sửa đổi và phân công cuối cùng.

dialog.note: Nghe thảo luận dự án để phân mục tiêu, giới hạn phép so và phân công cuối; không chọn ý đã bị sửa.

lines.t: We need to finish the plan for our design assignment. Are we still examining where people choose to sit in a small exhibition room? I know our tutor offered topics about sign lettering and ticket layout too, but neither explains why we started this project.

Yes, the seating question came from watching the volunteers repeatedly move chairs after visitors asked for a different position. That observation interested us more than the suggested topics. We must make clear that our exercise is a fictional classroom investigation, not a claim about visitors everywhere. We can build the model room ourselves.

A model will also let us move things without interrupting an actual exhibition. At first, I thought we needed a real gallery to make the exercise serious. The tutor pointed out that a controllable space was more useful for our narrow question than an impressive location with many differences we could not track.

That was good advice. In the first version, we asked people to choose the chair they liked best. Some chose one because it was nearest the exit, but others thought we meant the most comfortable chair. We used identical chairs, yet the wording invited answers to different questions.

So the revised task is to choose a place from which to read the small display label. We are interested in their choice of position, not a general judgement about comfort. Did the pilot show any problem with the diagram we give them before they enter?

Yes. Two people held it the opposite way round because the entrance was not marked. They thought the window symbol was the door. I have added an entrance arrow, but I don’t want to add photographs of every seat to the instructions; that might guide their choice before they see the room.

What about the window itself? The afternoon light makes one side much brighter. We originally planned to compare the chair near it with the chair by the opposite wall. That would change more than distance from the label.

We should cover the window and use the same room lights for every attempt. Then we can compare two positions with the label and chair type unchanged. It won’t remove every difference, but it will prevent one obvious change in light from being hidden inside the position comparison.

Our sheet has a column for time. Are we measuring how long they sit, or how long they take to choose? Those could tell very different stories. Someone might remain seated because they are waiting for us to speak.

We will time the choice only, from entering the room until they indicate a chair. That is not a measure of how much they enjoyed the room. We should avoid calling a quick decision better without knowing what led to it. We can keep the times as descriptions and ask for reasons afterwards.

The tutor also warned us about inviting only our friends. They already know one another and may discuss the activity before entering. I have written a short invitation for another class. We still won’t have a representative sample, but at least the group will not consist entirely of people who know our idea.

Agreed. And when we ask why they chose the chair, we should use a neutral question. “Was it because the light was better?” would put our explanation into their answer. Let’s say, “What influenced your choice?” and record the response before asking for clarification.

I can photograph the room before each round, since I will already be checking that the label remains in the same place. Could you prepare the results table and calculate the summary of choice times? We should each check the other’s entries afterwards rather than leave one person with all the verification.

Yes, I’ll handle the table. For the presentation, I’m less worried about filling the slides than about explaining what the exercise cannot show. We can describe the choices and the reasons offered, but we can’t claim that we have discovered the best seating plan for every exhibition. A clear limitation will be more useful than a dramatic conclusion. We should end by showing what another comparison would need to change.

items.q: 21. Why did the students choose the seating topic?
o: They noticed volunteers repeatedly moving chairs for visitors
It was the only topic on the tutor’s list
They wanted to study ticket prices
items.e: Nguồn hứng thú là quan sát chairs moved, không hai suggested topics.

items.q: 22. Why use a model room?
o: It offers control without interrupting a real exhibition
items.e: Mục tiêu hẹp cần controllable space, không prestige của gallery thật.

items.q: 23. What was wrong with “the chair they liked best”?
o: People interpreted the basis of liking differently
items.e: Comfort và proximity to exit cho thấy wording gọi các tiêu chí khác nhau.

items.q: 24. What confused two people in the pilot?
o: The diagram did not mark the entrance
They were shown photographs of every chair
items.e: Họ xoay sơ đồ vì lẫn window với door; arrow được thêm để sửa.

items.q: 25. Why cover the window?
o: To stop all visitors seeing the label
To create a more dramatic exhibition
To reduce a lighting difference in the position comparison
items.e: Giữ ánh sáng phòng giống giúp không nhập light vào biến position.

items.q: 26. What will be timed?
o: The entire time a person stays seated
The interval before a chair is selected
The total enjoyment of the room
items.e: From entering until indicate chair là định nghĩa measure được chốt.

items.q: 27. Why invite another class?
o: To reduce reliance on friends who know the idea
To claim a perfectly representative sample
To ensure everyone knows one another
items.e: Họ vẫn nhận không representative nhưng muốn tránh entirely friends.

items.q: 28. Which interview question do they prefer?
o: Why did you choose the obviously best chair?
items.e: Câu mở trung tính không đưa sẵn nguyên nhân hay đánh giá vào lời đáp.

items.q: 29. What will Tavin prepare?
o: The results table and summary of choice times
items.e: Nera nhận photos, Tavin nói I’ll handle the table sau lời nhờ.

items.q: 30. What is the main presentation concern?
o: Explaining the scope of what the exercise can show
items.e: Lượt cuối nhấn limits hơn dramatic conclusion và nêu phép so tiếp.

sections.h: Listening – Part 4 · How a collection acquires an order
sections.intro: Questions 31–40: hoàn thành ghi chú, ONE WORD ONLY cho mỗi câu. Bài giảng mô tả một dự án lớp học hư cấu, không phải kết quả nghiên cứu được công bố.

dialog.note: Nghe bài giảng theo giai đoạn và quan hệ giữa phương pháp, ví dụ, giới hạn; đọc ghi chú trước khi phát.

lines.t: Today I’ll discuss how an order is created when a small collection becomes a teaching resource. Our example is a fictional study called the Everyday Box Project. The team assembled forty ordinary objects made for this classroom exercise: folded papers, containers, pieces of cloth and simple models. The question was not who owned them or which was worth most. It was which relationships a classification would make visible, and which it would hide.

In the first stage, the group sorted the objects by material. Paper objects went together, cloth objects formed another group, and combined materials created a difficulty. This arrangement was easy to understand from a distance, but it separated objects that had been made for the same purpose. Two containers could end up in different groups because one was paper and the other cloth. The category was not wrong; it simply answered a particular question.

A second arrangement grouped objects by the action needed to make them. That moved some containers together and separated items that looked similar but were constructed differently. However, the team did not know the full making history of every object. They left uncertain cases marked rather than inventing a method from appearance. A visible seam, for example, might support a possibility without supplying a complete account of how an item was produced.

The third stage began with short recorded descriptions. Each maker was asked where the object had been used in the invented scenario. The team used location as another basis for grouping: objects from a kitchen setting, a work table or an outdoor gathering. This revealed connections that the material arrangement had missed. Yet it depended on an account supplied for the exercise. The recordings did not make the locations directly observable in the objects themselves.

The project therefore added a separate field for provenance. In this exercise, that meant recording where each account had come from and how it related to the object. It was important not to make the maker’s description, the observer’s inference and the organiser’s label sound like one voice. If the location was inferred rather than stated, the entry needed to show that difference. A neat category heading was no excuse for erasing the route by which information had been obtained.

The labels were kept provisional during the workshop. Participants could propose a different grouping, but they had to explain what their alternative revealed. Some wanted one object to appear in more than one group. Rather than force an immediate choice, the team made duplicate reference cards so that the original did not have to move constantly between tables. The cards were not extra objects; they were aids to representing more than one relationship.

Discussion often became most useful at the exceptions. An object that fitted easily into every familiar category did not necessarily teach more than an awkward case. A cloth container with a paper frame forced participants to say whether they were classifying surface, structure or function. The organisers recorded these explanations rather than count disagreement as a failure of the system. A category could remain useful while its boundary needed discussion.

At the review, the group compared the overlap between arrangements. The aim was not to prove that material, making method or location was the single natural order. It was to show that each arrangement offered a view. To preserve that history, the team saved each version of the catalogue instead of overwriting the earlier one. This made changes in their assumptions visible. A final tidy list alone would have hidden the decisions through which it emerged.

The teaching outcome was assessed through questions participants could now ask, not merely through speed in placing an object. Could they explain why a category was useful? Could they identify information the label did not contain? Could they suggest another relation without claiming that all previous work was mistaken? Those responses would give the next workshop a clearer purpose. The collection had become valuable as a resource for inquiry because its order could be examined and revised, not because one classification had ended the discussion.

items.q: 31. The project studied the ___ made visible by classification. (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: Mở đầu đối lập ownership/value với relationships được cách xếp làm hiện hoặc che.

items.q: 32. First arrangement: objects grouped by ___ (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: Giai đoạn đầu paper/cloth/combined materials, không purpose.

items.q: 33. Unknown making methods were marked as ___ rather than invented. (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: Team left uncertain cases marked, không đoán lịch sử từ hình thức.

items.q: 34. Recorded descriptions supported grouping by ___ (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: Kitchen/work table/outdoor gathering là địa điểm dùng được nêu trong lời ghi.

items.q: 35. A separate field recorded the ___ of each account. (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: Trường provenance ghi nguồn lời kể và quan hệ với vật, tách nguồn khỏi suy luận.

items.q: 36. Labels remained ___ during the workshop. (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: Provisional giữ khả năng sửa khi người tham gia đề nghị quan hệ khác.

items.q: 37. Discussion was often productive at the ___ (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: Awkward mixed case buộc nêu phân loại surface/structure/function nên exceptions hữu ích.

items.q: 38. Review compared the ___ between arrangements. (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: Overlap là phần nhóm gặp nhau qua các cách xếp, không chọn một natural order.

items.q: 39. The team saved each ___ of the catalogue. (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: Giữ từng version thay overwrite để thấy đổi giả định và quyết định.

items.q: 40. Learning was assessed through the ___ participants could ask. (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: Kết bài dùng questions có thể đặt thay chỉ tốc độ xếp vật làm tiêu chí học.

sections.h: Reading – Passage 1 · A reading room that travels
sections.intro: Questions 1–13. Đọc A–H. Với câu TRUE/FALSE/NOT GIVEN, xét đúng nội dung chứ không kiến thức ngoài. Câu điền dùng đúng giới hạn từ; câu heading chọn chức năng chính đoạn.

read.title: A reading room that travels
read.text:
A. The fictional Lenvari reading house closed its main room for repairs at the beginning of April. The collection was safe, but visitors could no longer browse the shelves. Instead of suspending the service until September, staff designed a travelling reading room that could visit two neighbourhood halls and a workshop. It was not a vehicle carrying a complete library. The books travelled in a small set of movable cases, and the host building supplied tables, chairs and a place to store empty boxes during each visit.

B. Each case opened into two shallow shelves. When closed, it could be moved on detachable wheels, but the wheels were removed before visitors approached it. The first prototype opened on only one side, which created a queue and made it difficult for two people to browse together. The revised version could be opened from either side. Staff did not claim that this design would suit every building. Before a first visit, they checked the available floor space and agreed where the cases could be placed without blocking another activity.

C. The travelling collection contained two hundred and forty books. One hundred and twenty were adult fiction, sixty were children’s stories and sixty supported practical learning activities. The team considered taking only the most frequently borrowed titles, then rejected that rule. It would have made the selection familiar but narrow. They included a small number of less frequently borrowed works and invited hosts to suggest subjects for the next visit. A suggestion was not a promise that every requested title would be available immediately.

D. The route followed a regular pattern. On Tuesdays the cases went to Neralin Hall; on Wednesdays they visited the smaller Talvori room. Saturday mornings were reserved for the workshop, where a short reading activity could accompany browsing. Staff originally considered a Friday evening visit there, but the host already used the space for another group. The public notice gave only the confirmed schedule. It did not include provisional dates discussed during planning, because people needed to know when they could actually find the books.

E. Borrowing used a numbered paper card rather than a new digital system. Visitors with an existing reading-house card could continue to use it. A new reader received a temporary number at the host desk and could borrow two books. The number linked the loan to the service record; it was not printed beside a reader’s comments in the public display. Returns could be made at either hall on a scheduled visit. The workshop did not store returns between Saturdays, so the notice explained that limit rather than letting visitors leave books outside a closed door.

F. Volunteers at the host buildings were given a short introduction before the first visit. Their role was to explain the borrowing steps and show where different subjects were placed, not to recommend a title they had never read. A simple picture guide helped visitors follow the order of borrowing. Written explanations were available in two languages chosen for this invented setting. If a visitor needed another form of support, the volunteer recorded the request for staff to consider rather than pretending that the existing guide served every person equally well.

G. The first Tuesday attracted forty-one visits, while a later Saturday attracted seventy-two. These figures showed use of the service, but they were not a direct test of which host was better. Saturday included a workshop, and its opening period was longer. The records also counted visits rather than distinct people, so someone returning after lunch could appear twice. Staff retained the numbers with those definitions attached. They did not turn a useful service record into a claim that every visitor had borrowed a book or preferred the mobile cases to the original shelves.

H. Feedback brought a further design change. Some readers wanted a place to look at a book before deciding whether to borrow it, and the shallow cases offered no suitable surface for that. Hosts therefore agreed to keep one table free as a browsing table. It was a modest alteration, but it connected the cases with the way people actually used them. Before the main room reopened, staff planned to review the route, the selection and the work involved. They might retain some visits afterwards, but the temporary service had not yet become a permanent promise.

items.q: 1. The cases carried the entire reading-house collection.
items.e: A nêu không phải complete library; C chỉ tập chọn hai trăm bốn mươi sách.

items.q: 2. The first prototype could be browsed from both sides.
items.e: B ghi prototype opened on only one side; revised version mới hai phía.

items.q: 3. The collection included books that were not among the most frequently borrowed.
items.e: C nêu included less frequently borrowed works sau khi bác quy tắc chỉ title phổ biến.

items.q: 4. The text states the purchase price of each movable case.
items.e: Không đoạn nào cung cấp giá case; không được suy từ design hoặc work.

items.q: 5. The two written languages were selected after a survey of every resident.
items.e: F nói chosen for invented setting nhưng không nêu khảo sát toàn dân.

items.q: 6. Tuesday destination: ___ Hall. (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: D gắn Tuesday với Neralin, Wednesday với Talvori.

items.q: 7. A new reader may borrow ___ books. (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: E cho temporary number và limit two books; không lấy số hall làm hạn mượn.

items.q: 8. Returns are not stored at the ___ between Saturdays. (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: E phân hall scheduled visits với workshop không giữ ngoài lịch.

items.q: 9. Choose the best heading for paragraph C.
o: A selection broader than popularity alone
A complete transfer of every book
An immediate guarantee for every request
items.e: C giải thích tập chọn có works ít mượn và không hứa mọi yêu cầu ngay.

items.q: 10. Choose the best heading for paragraph G.
o: Proof that the largest host is always best
Keeping the meaning of a service count clear
items.e: G giữ numbers nhưng nêu session/definition limits, không bỏ đếm.

items.q: 11. What was a host volunteer expected to do?
o: Guarantee all visitors had identical support
Recommend every book as though personally read
items.e: F xác định role thủ tục và chỉ vị trí, không fake expertise.

items.q: 12. Why is forty-one versus seventy-two not a direct host comparison?
o: The sessions differed in activity and length
The same person could never return
items.e: G nêu workshop và longer opening; visits cũng không distinct people.

items.q: 13. What change resulted from feedback?
o: A table was kept free for browsing
items.e: H nêu browsing table đáp nhu cầu xem trước, future service vẫn review.

sections.h: Reading – Passage 2 · A symbol is an agreement
sections.intro: Questions 14–26. Chọn heading theo chức năng cả đoạn; TRUE/FALSE/NOT GIVEN chỉ theo nguồn. Với câu điền, ONE WORD ONLY. Dự án và đảo đều hư cấu; không suy quy tắc văn hóa phổ quát từ ví dụ.

read.title: A symbol is an agreement
read.text:
A. A diagram can look simple because it leaves things out. That is not necessarily a weakness. A map showing every visible feature at equal weight would be difficult to use for a particular journey. The question is which omissions serve the reader’s purpose and which remove information the reader needs. A symbol is part of that choice. Its shape does not carry a complete meaning by itself; the diagram, its key and the task establish how it should be read. Familiarity may help, but a designer should not assume that every reader brings the same familiarity.

B. The invented Naleri Path Project explored this problem using a map of an imaginary island. The island contained a village, a garden, a store house and several paths. In the first design, a continuous blue line connected the village and garden. The team intended it to mark a recommended walking route. They chose blue because it separated the route from the black outlines of buildings. They had not included water on the island, so they did not expect a reader to interpret the line as a stream. Their expectation was not the same as a tested agreement.

C. Twelve volunteers saw that version without a key. Six described the line as water, four identified it as a route and two said they could not decide. These answers did not establish what blue means in every culture or every map. The group was small, and the task invited a quick interpretation of one invented design. It did, however, show a specific mismatch between the team’s intention and several readers’ interpretations. Saying that the symbol was obvious would now require ignoring responses the designers had actually collected.

D. The next version added a key stating that the line was a recommended route. A different group of fourteen volunteers then used the map. Most identified the intended meaning, but the team could not attribute every difference to the key alone: the groups differed, and the second task gave readers more time. The report stated the new result with those limits. It did not describe the first volunteers as careless or the later group as more intelligent. The relevant question concerned support provided by the design, not a ranking of the people who tried it.

E. Meaning was only one issue. A route could be understood correctly and still fail to answer the question a reader had. One task asked for the shortest path between two places. Another asked for a route passing a quiet stopping point. The same recommendation was not necessarily best for both. The project therefore revised its wording from “the best route” to “the route recommended for this task”. This was a small change in language but a substantial change in what the designer claimed to know about the reader’s priorities.

F. A second symbol produced a similar discussion. The team used a dashed line for a boundary whose position in the invented story was uncertain. Some readers treated it as another path. The designers could have rejected those readings as mistakes, but instead they added an explanation of the line style. They also preserved earlier versions of the map so that the reason for the change would remain visible. A final clean image would show the chosen convention without showing why the convention needed to be made explicit.

G. The exercise also considered alternative forms of access. A spoken description could name the stops in order, while a raised-line version could represent selected spatial relationships. Neither would automatically reproduce every feature of the printed map. The team would need to decide which information mattered for the intended activity and test whether that information was available in the alternative form. Simply converting the appearance of a symbol would not settle whether the reader could use it for the same purpose.

H. The project ended without declaring one universal colour or line style. Its outcome was a way of asking clearer questions. What should the reader be able to find? Which convention must be explained? What does the key supply that the shape alone does not? A diagram becomes more usable when its designer can answer such questions and revise the claim when readers reveal a mismatch. Simplicity remains valuable, but it should be the result of a well-defined purpose, not an excuse for leaving an essential agreement unstated.

items.q: 14. Best heading for paragraph B?
o: A key that already solved every problem
An untested assumption in a first design
items.e: B nêu designer expects blue route vì không có water, chưa kiểm reader.

items.q: 15. Best heading for paragraph C?
o: A local mismatch rather than a universal rule
Proof of a colour’s meaning in every culture
A competition won by the fastest volunteers
items.e: C giới hạn sample nhưng cho thấy intention khác responses.

items.q: 16. Best heading for paragraph E?
o: One best route for every priority
Why all route labels should be removed
Correct interpretation can still answer the wrong task
items.e: Hiểu route đúng chưa bảo đảm đáp shortest/quiet priorities.

items.q: 17. Best heading for paragraph H?
o: A rejection of simplicity in every diagram
Clearer questions instead of a universal convention
The final choice of a colour for all maps
items.e: H tổng kết cách hỏi purpose/key/convention, vẫn nhận simplicity có ích.

items.q: 18. The first map included a river between village and garden.
items.e: B nói không đưa water lên đảo; blue line intended route.

items.q: 19. The first group contained volunteers from twelve different countries.
items.e: C cho số twelve volunteers, không cung cấp countries hoặc nationality.

items.q: 20. The second group had more time for the task.
items.e: D nêu second task gave readers more time, là một giới hạn so.

items.q: 21. All volunteers preferred the raised-line version to print.
items.e: G bàn alternative access, không có thử sở thích toàn volunteers.

items.q: 22. The second map added a ___ explaining the blue line. (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: D dùng key xác định recommended route, không chỉ đổi shape.

items.q: 23. The dashed line indicated an uncertain ___ (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: F giải thích dashed boundary uncertain, một số người nhầm path.

items.q: 24. Earlier map ___ were preserved to show why changes occurred. (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: F giữ earlier versions để lịch sử quy ước còn thấy.

items.q: 25. Why avoid calling later readers more intelligent?
o: The first group answered every question correctly
Intelligence was measured by the blue line
The aim concerns design support and the comparison has other differences
items.e: D bác ranking people vì groups/time/design khác; không có test trí tuệ.

items.q: 26. What must an alternative access format be tested for?
o: Whether it removes the need to define purpose
Whether it makes information needed for the activity available
Whether it copies every printed feature exactly
items.e: G nhấn intended information/task, không appearance conversion tự đủ.

sections.h: Reading – Passage 3 · When a longer record tells us less
sections.intro: Questions 27–40. Với YES/NO/NOT GIVEN, xét quan điểm/thông tin người viết đã nêu, không suy từ kiến thức ngoài. Câu điền ONE WORD ONLY. Dự án biểu diễn là tình huống tự tạo cho bài đọc.

read.title: When a longer record tells us less
read.text:
A. The desire for a complete record is understandable. If every stage of an activity is preserved, later readers may hope to judge it without depending on a summary. A longer recording can indeed allow a question that its maker did not anticipate. Yet length alone does not make a record self-explanatory. A camera has a position, a written log has categories and a microphone has a location. Preserving more material can reduce some omissions while leaving the conditions of recording just as important as before.

B. An invented project at the Meralen performance class illustrates the difficulty. Four rehearsal recordings, each lasting half an hour, were saved for a review of how a final scene had developed. The group also prepared a twelve-minute selection. One proposal called the full two hours the reliable record and the selection merely promotional. That distinction assumed that unedited duration supplied understanding while selection could only conceal. Before accepting it, the reviewers asked what each version allowed a viewer to find out.

C. The full recordings showed interruptions, repeated attempts and discussions that the selection omitted. For a question about how long the group spent on a transition, those details mattered. A viewer could locate attempts and compare their order. For a question about why a cue changed, however, the relevant explanation was not always spoken near the visible alteration. One discussion referred to a comment made outside the recorded session. More minutes did not create a statement that had never been captured. The record had a boundary even when no internal passage was removed.

D. The selected version placed three attempts beside one another. This made a change in timing easier to notice, but it also imposed a comparison that the original sequence did not present in that form. Rather than label the selection wholly trustworthy or wholly deceptive, the team attached an editing log. It identified the source of each segment and explained why it had been included. The log did not make the edit neutral; it made the choice available for examination. A viewer could then return to a longer section if the question required it.

E. Captions introduced another layer. A line saying that a performer “realised the mistake” described an inner state, not simply a visible change in movement. The performer had not used that expression in the recorded discussion. The team replaced it with a description of the action and attributed the explanation that came from a later conversation. This was not a demand to remove every interpretation from the record. It was a way to distinguish an observed sequence, a reported intention and the editor’s inference so that a fluent label did not silently exchange one for another.

F. Different viewers were then given different tasks. Some were asked to reconstruct the order of revisions; others were asked to compare how the final cue worked. The full version helped with some sequencing questions, while the selection helped viewers see the three attempts together. Neither result established one version as best for every purpose. The tasks affected which omissions mattered. An account of the comparison therefore needed to report the questions asked, not simply announce that viewers had learned more from one format.

G. Access to the recordings also depended on the group’s agreement. Participants had allowed a teaching review, not unrestricted distribution of every remark. The fact that a longer record could answer more questions did not automatically create permission to circulate it more widely. The group prepared a separate version for visitors and checked which statements could be included. This restriction limited available evidence, but concealing the restriction would have been more misleading than stating it. A record can be useful while acknowledging that not every reader has access to every part.

H. There was a practical cost as well. Keeping a file was only the beginning of making it usable. Someone had to describe its date, its relation to other versions and the conditions under which it could be examined. A folder of recordings with unexplained names would shift the work of reconstruction onto later users. The project therefore saved fewer duplicates and spent more time documenting the remaining versions. It did not assume that the largest archive would necessarily offer the clearest route through the activity.

I. The lesson is not that shorter records are superior. It is that a record should be judged by the questions it can support and the limits it makes visible. Selection, description and access all require decisions, whether the material is brief or extensive. A responsible account enables readers to inspect those decisions rather than promises a view from nowhere. More material may be valuable, but its value emerges through a relation between evidence, purpose and explanation, not through duration alone.

items.q: 27. What assumption is challenged in paragraph B?
o: That unedited length is automatically reliable while selection can only conceal
That there are four rehearsal recordings
items.e: B đặt reliable full/promotional selection thành assumption cần kiểm, không bác sự tồn tại recording.

items.q: 28. What could extra minutes not provide?
o: The order of attempts already recorded
Any evidence that an interruption occurred
An explanation never captured in the sessions
items.e: C có comment outside session nên duration không tự thêm missing statement.

items.q: 29. What does the editing log achieve?
o: It proves the full recordings useless
items.e: D nói choice available for examination, không remove interpretation.

items.q: 30. Why replace “realised the mistake”?
o: It presented an unspoken inner state as though directly observed
It was too short for the caption
items.e: E tách action thấy và explanation later attribution khỏi inference nội tâm.

items.q: 31. The writer believes that a longer record is always self-explanatory.
items.e: A bác length alone self-explanatory, I bác duration alone.

items.q: 32. The project received funding from a national museum.
items.e: Không cung cấp tổ chức tài trợ; không suy từ class/project.

items.q: 33. Information about selection can help readers examine an edit.
items.e: D giữ source segments và reasons qua editing log để kiểm choices.

items.q: 34. The writer argues that all interpretation should be removed from a record.
items.e: E nói rõ not demand to remove every interpretation, cần phân loại.

items.q: 35. Every participant later became a professional performer.
items.e: Nguồn không nói nghề về sau, không suy từ lớp performance.

items.q: 36. The full version helped answer some questions about ___ (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: F nêu full helped some sequencing questions, không mọi task.

items.q: 37. The team attached an editing ___ to the selection. (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: D dùng editing log ghi source và reason của mỗi segment.

items.q: 38. A longer record does not automatically give ___ for wider circulation. (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: G phân khả năng trả lời thêm với quyền chia sẻ theo agreement.

items.q: 39. Best heading for paragraph H?
o: The work needed to make an archive usable
Why all files should be duplicated indefinitely
A technical ranking of recording equipment
items.e: H nói metadata, relation, conditions và công mô tả, không equipment.

items.q: 40. Which statement best represents the final argument?
o: Avoid judgement because every record is partial
Judge a record through purpose, support and visible limits
items.e: I bác cả shortest rule và promise view from nowhere, vẫn đánh giá qua câu hỏi.

sections.intro: Khoảng 20 phút; tối thiểu 150 từ. Biểu đồ và mẫu đều tự soạn.

write.task: The line chart shows the percentage of participants choosing three learning formats at a fictional centre in 2018, 2020, 2022 and 2024. Summarise the main features and make relevant comparisons. Write at least 150 words. Các số liệu tự đặt; không thêm nguyên nhân hoặc tổng người khi biểu đồ chỉ cho tỉ trọng.

chart.title: Learning format selected at the fictional Orelan centre

write.model: The line chart compares the proportions of participants selecting a single workshop, a small-group course or a self-guided activity at the fictional Orelan centre between 2018 and 2024. Overall, small-group courses became increasingly popular and were the leading format from 2020 onwards. The share choosing a single workshop declined throughout, while self-guided activities remained stable before a modest final rise. In 2018, single workshops accounted for forty per cent of participants, five percentage points more than small-group courses. Over the next six years, the workshop share fell first to thirty-five per cent, then thirty, and finally twenty. By contrast, small-group courses rose in equal steps from thirty-five to fifty per cent. They overtook workshops in 2020 and ended the period with a lead of thirty percentage points. Self-guided activities represented one quarter of selections in each of the first three years. Their share then increased to thirty per cent in 2024, placing them above workshops but still twenty points below small-group courses. The chart describes the distribution of choices rather than the total number of participants, so it does not establish whether overall enrolment increased.
write.modelVi: Biểu đồ so tỉ trọng chọn workshop đơn, khóa nhóm nhỏ và hoạt động tự học tại Orelan hư cấu từ 2018 đến 2024. Nhóm nhỏ tăng, dẫn từ 2020; workshop giảm suốt, tự học ổn định rồi tăng nhẹ. Năm đầu workshop bốn mươi phần trăm, hơn nhóm nhỏ năm điểm. Workshop lần lượt xuống ba mươi lăm, ba mươi rồi hai mươi; nhóm nhỏ tăng đều ba mươi lăm lên năm mươi, vượt năm 2020 và cuối hơn ba mươi điểm. Tự học một phần tư ba năm đầu, cuối ba mươi, hơn workshop và kém nhóm nhỏ hai mươi điểm. Đây là cơ cấu chứ không tổng người nên không xác định tổng ghi danh tăng.
rubric: Task achievement: overview rõ, chọn xu hướng và so đúng số/đơn vị, tối thiểu 150 từ.
Coherence and cohesion: nhóm dữ kiện theo hướng thay đổi, liên kết không lặp máy móc.
Lexical resource: dùng share/proportion/percentage points chính xác, không bịa nguyên nhân.
Grammatical range and accuracy: phối câu so sánh và mốc quá khứ đúng; tự rà mạo từ, chia động từ.

sections.intro: Khoảng 40 phút; tối thiểu 250 từ. Thảo luận hai views và nêu ý kiến. Mẫu không phải bài nên học thuộc.

write.task: Some people believe that public learning centres should offer a few long courses, while others think they should provide many short workshops. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons and relevant examples from your knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
write.model: Long courses and short workshops serve different needs, so a public learning centre should not choose between them solely by counting how many activities appear in its programme. I favour a combination in which short introductions lead to sustained learning where demand and resources justify it. Those who prefer long courses can point to continuity. A learner may need time to practise, receive feedback and attempt a task again. In an imagined writing course, a participant could develop a story over several weeks rather than leave with only a first draft. A continuing group can also make responsibilities and expectations more predictable. However, a long commitment may exclude people whose schedules change or who do not yet know whether the subject suits them. Supporters of short workshops therefore have a strong case for access. A brief session allows someone to try a skill without promising several months. It can also respond to a specific question, such as how to organise a small personal collection. Yet a programme full of introductions may leave interested learners with no next step, and a crowded list of events is not evidence that everyone can participate meaningfully. I would use short workshops as entry points and review which topics need a longer sequence. The decision should consider feedback from those who attended and those who could not, the kind of practice required and the work available from tutors. A centre could then offer selected continuing courses rather than expand every popular introduction automatically. This approach preserves low-commitment opportunities while recognising that some learning depends on time and revision. The aim should be a coherent route through the programme, not the greatest number of sessions or the longest course in isolation.
write.modelVi: Khóa dài và workshop ngắn đáp nhu cầu khác; trung tâm không nên chọn chỉ theo số hoạt động in chương trình. Tôi chọn kết hợp, giới thiệu ngắn dẫn sang học bền khi nhu cầu/nguồn lực hợp. Khóa dài có liên tục để luyện, nhận góp ý và thử lại, như truyện phát triển vài tuần, nhóm ổn cho trách nhiệm rõ. Nhưng cam kết dài có thể loại người lịch đổi hoặc chưa biết hợp môn. Workshop ngắn cho thử không hứa nhiều tháng và đáp câu hỏi riêng như tổ chức bộ sưu tập. Tuy vậy toàn nhập môn có thể không có bước sau; lịch dày chưa chứng minh tham gia có ý nghĩa. Tôi dùng workshop làm cửa vào và review chủ đề cần chuỗi dài, xét người đã/không dự, kiểu luyện và công tutor. Chọn một số khóa tiếp nối thay tự mở rộng mọi buổi đông. Cách này giữ cơ hội ít cam kết và nhận việc học cần thời gian/sửa. Mục tiêu là lộ trình mạch lạc, không nhiều buổi nhất hoặc dài nhất.
rubric: Task response: phát triển lý do cả hai quan điểm và lập trường riêng, tối thiểu 250 từ.
Coherence and cohesion: đoạn có chức năng và lý do nối kết luận, không chỉ liệt kê hai phía.
Lexical resource: từ về chương trình, cam kết và tiếp cận đúng nghĩa, ví dụ giả được nhận là giả.
Grammatical range and accuracy: kết hợp so sánh, điều kiện và nhượng bộ có kiểm soát; sửa lỗi gây mơ hồ.

sections.intro: Người hỏi chọn câu về ghi chú và nơi đọc, hỏi tiếp tự nhiên khi phù hợp. Mẫu là ví dụ tự soạn, người học trả lời theo bản thân.

tasks.p: Do you enjoy making notes when you learn something?
tasks.model: Usually, yes, but I keep them selective. If I try to write down every sentence, I stop following the explanation. I prefer a few keywords and an example that shows how the idea works.

tasks.p: Do you prefer handwritten or typed notes?
tasks.model: For a first explanation I often write by hand because I can draw a quick connection between ideas. If I need to reorganise the notes later, typing is more convenient. The task matters more than a fixed preference.

tasks.p: Have your note-taking habits changed?
tasks.model: Yes. I used to collect pages without reviewing them. Now I leave a space for questions and return to the notes after trying the task. That makes a shorter set more useful to me.

tasks.p: What kind of place do you like to read in?
tasks.model: I like a place that is quiet enough to concentrate but not completely isolated. A small shared reading room can work well, provided people can move without constantly interrupting one another.

tasks.p: Do you ever discuss what you read with other people?
tasks.model: Yes, especially when a story leaves something unexplained. Someone else may notice a detail I missed. I do not need us to agree at the end, but I enjoy understanding why our readings differ.

tasks.p: Would you join a short workshop on a new skill?
tasks.model: I would, if it gave me a realistic idea of what I could try afterwards. A brief session is a useful way to explore a subject before making a longer commitment.

rubric: Trả lời trực tiếp rồi phát triển vừa đủ theo câu hỏi Part 1.
Từ và thì phù hợp thói quen, so sánh, thay đổi; không ép đoạn thuộc mọi đề.
Ghi âm để kiểm độ dễ theo, âm cuối và trọng tâm, không tự quy đổi band từ một câu.

sections.intro: Thẻ nói dài nối với chủ đề học kỹ năng và cải thiện đồ vật. Không học thuộc câu chuyện mẫu như trải nghiệm thật của mình.

tasks.p: Describe an object that you changed to make it more useful. You should say what it was, why you changed it, what you did, and explain how the change affected its use. Có một phút chuẩn bị; nói một đến hai phút. Nếu dùng tình huống giả để luyện, hãy nêu rõ.
tasks.model: For this practice, I’ll describe an imagined change to a small box used for drawing materials. At first, the box had one large space, so the pencils, paper pieces and short rulers mixed together. It looked tidy when the lid was closed, but finding one item often meant taking everything out. The owner decided to add three removable dividers made from folded card. Before fixing them in position, the owner tried two arrangements with the materials actually inside. The first left a long narrow section that was difficult to reach, while the second kept the most frequently used items near the front. A small paper label was added to each section, but the dividers were left removable because the collection might change. The useful part was not simply making the box look more organised. It reduced the number of things that had to be moved when looking for a particular tool. There was still a limitation: large paper sheets did not fit, so they needed a separate folder. I would choose this example because it shows a modest improvement based on use, rather than a complete redesign that only looks impressive in a photograph.

rubric: Phát triển đủ bốn gợi ý cue card trong mạch sự việc, không chỉ bốn câu rời.
Nêu lý do, thử và kết quả cùng giới hạn bằng từ cụ thể; câu chuyện thật của người học không cần giống mẫu.
Kiểm thời lượng khi nói thực, nhịp và tự sửa ngắn; chữ mẫu không bảo đảm đúng hai phút trên mọi giọng.

sections.intro: Thảo luận mở rộng từ đồ vật sang học tập, tính độc lập và đánh giá. Người hỏi có thể thêm Why? hoặc phản ví dụ liên quan.

tasks.p: Why do people sometimes change ordinary objects instead of replacing them?
tasks.model: Sometimes the object already fits most of their needs, so a small change solves the remaining difficulty more directly than starting again. There may also be personal reasons to keep it. However, I would not assume that modification is always better. The time required and the quality of the result matter. A sensible choice depends on what the change enables, rather than a general rule that keeping or replacing is morally superior.

tasks.p: How can a workshop help people become more independent learners?
tasks.model: It can give them a way to test a decision, not only a set of steps to repeat. For instance, a tutor might ask learners to compare two arrangements and explain which one suits a purpose. That explanation can help them adapt when the next object differs. Still, one successful workshop does not prove that everyone can work independently in every setting. I would look for a learner trying a new case and identifying when further help is needed.

tasks.p: Are short workshops better than long courses?
tasks.model: I would ask what the learner needs at that stage. A short workshop can lower the commitment required to explore a subject. A longer course can provide repeated practice and feedback that a single introduction cannot. The problem is not choosing one format as universally better, but making the route between them clear. A centre could offer an introduction and then explain what continued practice involves, rather than leave people with either a large commitment or no next step.

tasks.p: How should organisers judge whether a learning activity was successful?
tasks.model: They should begin with the intended learning, then use evidence that relates to it. Attendance shows that people came, but not what they understood or could do afterwards. A finished object can be useful evidence, although it may hide assistance. I would combine a small amount of work, an explanation and feedback about access. The evaluation should remain proportionate: collecting endless records that nobody examines would not improve the judgement simply by increasing its size.

rubric: Phát triển ý trừu tượng theo tiêu chí và ví dụ, phản hồi câu hỏi tiếp thay vì đọc bài Task 2.
Giữ mức khái quát có phạm vi; so sánh và nhượng bộ có chức năng thật.

tests.title: IELTS Academic – Đề tự soạn số 4
tests.intro: Đề luyện tự soạn, có 4 phần Listening/40 câu, 3 bài Reading/40 câu, 2 Writing và 3 phần Speaking. Mọi người, tổ chức, địa điểm, tình huống và số liệu trong đề đều đặt cho bài tập. Đây không phải đề thi chính thức hay công cụ quy đổi điểm chứng chỉ. Reading khoảng 60 phút; Writing 60 phút, Task 1 ít nhất 150 từ và Task 2 ít nhất 250 từ. Nghe một lượt cho mỗi phần khi tự mô phỏng; thời lượng phát còn tùy giọng TTS của thiết bị, giáo viên cần kiểm tốc độ và khoảng nghỉ trước khi dùng có bấm giờ. Đáp án giải thích theo ngữ liệu, không dựa kiến thức bên ngoài. Kết quả dùng để tìm lỗi theo kỹ năng; không bảo đảm band thi thật.

sections.intro: Questions 1–10. Điền thông tin cuối được chốt theo giới hạn từng câu. Buổi học, tên, phí và nơi đều được đặt cho bài luyện.

dialog.note: Theo cuộc đặt buổi vẽ để tách lịch còn chỗ, số người giảm và vật cần tự mang; chú ý thông tin của khóa khác.

lines.t: Hello. I’d like to ask about the observation drawing session at the fictional Toralin Model House. A few members of our reading group want to try drawing objects, and I saw that you welcome complete beginners. We are not looking for a photography session.

You have the right activity. We use simple models and ask people to look carefully before making a sketch. It is an introduction, not a course that promises to turn everyone into an experienced artist in an afternoon. May I take one contact name for the group?

Certainly. My surname is Torvane. That is T, O, R, V, A, N, E. There is no second R. I can collect the group’s questions, but I would prefer you to explain any changes clearly because I will pass the details on in writing.

Thank you. The session you may have seen advertised on Tuesday is now full. There is space on Sunday. It follows the same beginner plan, but the tutor has asked for a smaller group so there is time to discuss what each person noticed.

Sunday should work. We first had twelve interested people, but three can no longer attend. Please reserve nine places rather than keep those extra three for us. We can tell the others about another session when a new date is announced.

Nine places are available. The session starts at two fifteen in the afternoon. An earlier message said two, but we added time between activities so the tutor can reset the models. Please don’t arrive at one fifteen expecting an hour of preparation; reception will still be supporting another group.

I’ll write two fifteen. What room should we ask for? We visited once for a reading event and used a large upstairs room, but one member of this group would prefer to stay on the ground floor if that is possible.

This session is in the Alveri room, which is on the ground floor. It is not the room used for most reading events. From reception, follow the short corridor and stop at the second door. The first door leads to a storage room, so please do not join anyone moving equipment there.

That sounds manageable. How much does the introduction cost? One friend mentioned twenty pounds from a previous visit, and another saw a price of twenty-five for a longer course. I assume neither is necessarily the current beginner fee.

Correct. This particular session is twenty-two pounds per person in our invented booking. It includes paper and a simple practice sheet. The longer course uses different materials and meets more than once. Please do not pay for that course just to reserve this one afternoon; the activities have separate lists.
What should people bring? Most have a pen and a notebook, but I’m not sure whether those are suitable. We don’t want to arrive carrying a large set of equipment that we will not use.

Ask everyone to bring a pencil. We provide the paper, and there is no need for a new sketchbook. A pen can be useful for notes afterwards, but it is not the tool used in the first exercises. The tutor wants people to revise a line without feeling that every mark must be permanent.

What objects will we draw? It may help the group understand that we are starting with observation rather than trying to invent a complete scene from memory. We would rather know the actual plan than imagine something far more complicated.

The main models are small boats made from plain card. They have a few visible folds and no printed decoration. We used bottles last month, but not for this session. There will be more than one view, and the tutor will ask people to compare what changes when they move their seat.
Do you need the final list before Sunday? I can send first names, but I have not asked everyone whether they want to show their sketches at the end. I don’t want to promise that for them.

A name list is enough for the booking. Please confirm it by Friday. Saturday is too late for the tutor’s seating plan, even though the activity is on Sunday. Showing a sketch is optional, and the tutor will ask again during the session rather than rely on your booking to grant permission.

Where should the whole group meet? If nine people wait inside the corridor, we may block the other activity. I can give everyone one meeting point so we do not keep asking reception where the others are.

Use the side entrance as your meeting point. It has a covered space and does not interrupt the main reception queue. When everyone has arrived, one person can check in for the group. Please keep the doorway itself clear so other visitors can enter.

Thank you. I’ll confirm nine names by Friday, ask them to bring pencils and meet at the side entrance before the Sunday session at two fifteen. If anything changes, I’ll contact reception rather than assume there is a spare place.

That is the confirmed arrangement. We look forward to seeing your group in the Alveri room. The aim is to practise looking and comparing, so nobody needs to arrive with a finished drawing to prove they belong in the beginner session.

sections.h: Listening – Part 2 · An indoor model-garden orientation
sections.intro: Questions 11–20. Theo hướng dẫn tham quan hư cấu để chọn nơi, giờ và quyền sử dụng đúng; câu điền theo giới hạn ghi riêng.

dialog.note: Nghe hướng dẫn tại triển lãm mô hình để phân lộ trình, phòng yên, mẫu thực hành được cầm và tác phẩm chỉ quan sát.

lines.t: Good afternoon and welcome to the fictional Vareli Model Garden. Despite its name, this is an indoor exhibition made from paper, card and cloth; it is not a collection of living plants. The purpose is to compare ways of representing a place. Two makers can start with the same invented garden and emphasise very different features. You do not need gardening knowledge to explore the displays, and no model is presented as a practical plan for planting outside.

At reception you can collect a folded plan. A star marks the information point, while circles mark the three rooms used in today’s short tour. The circles do not mean that those rooms are the most important exhibits. They simply show where the group will stop. If you prefer to look around independently, the plan lists the other rooms too. Please keep it folded away from the models; an open sheet can easily brush a delicate part when someone turns.

We begin in the Varel room, directly opposite reception. This room presents the same path in three different scales. The smallest model leaves out individual seats, while the largest shows their position. That difference is useful, not necessarily a mistake. The makers had different questions in mind. The label asks you to consider what each scale makes available to a viewer rather than choose the most detailed one as the automatic winner.

The room to the left contains visitors’ draft designs from earlier workshops. It is sometimes used for discussion, so it is not our quiet area. If you want to sit and read descriptions without a group activity nearby, use the room behind the central display. It has a short written guide and ordinary seats. The room on the right is a store, and visitors should not enter it even if staff leave the door open while moving boxes.

Today’s demonstration will begin at one forty. A leaflet printed before the programme was final gives two, and an old wall notice says one thirty. Please follow the current time of one forty. You can join without making a separate reservation, but the demonstration uses a small table, so we may ask people to stand back after the close view. The facilitator will repeat the view from another angle rather than promise that everyone can crowd around at once.

If you would like to examine a detail, magnifiers are available at the observation desk. The shop sells postcards but does not lend equipment. Return a magnifier to the observation desk before leaving the gallery. It is useful for seeing marks in the card, but please do not use it to press a model flat. The object remains on its support throughout. Ask a volunteer if the position makes a feature difficult to see.

There is a separate set of practice models on the low table near the workshop entrance. You may handle those after reading the short instruction card. This permission does not extend to the exhibition models. The practice set is intended to let you compare folds and joins by touch, while the displayed pieces remain in their chosen arrangement. A label at each table distinguishes the two sets, so please check rather than assume that every paper object can be picked up.

Photography today follows a simple invented exhibition agreement. Models with a green card may be photographed for personal reference; a red card means please ask at reception first. The cards do not rank the quality of the work. Some makers are still deciding how a draft should be shown, and staff need to check the agreed use. Even where photography is allowed, leave enough room for other visitors to look instead of using a camera as a reason to occupy the whole front of a display.

We welcome people interested in volunteering for future visits. The first task is usually helping a new visitor use the plan, not immediately leading the full tour. You can leave your available times on the volunteer sheet at reception. There is no requirement to have made an elaborate model yourself. Careful listening and a willingness to ask when uncertain are more useful than pretending to know every maker’s intention.

Before you go, use the question box by the exit if a description leaves something unclear. We are interested in the questions the exhibition raises, not only praise or a general score. Today’s guided tour covers selected comparisons rather than every room. Afterwards, you can return to a model that interested you and follow another route through the plan. We hope you leave with a clearer way to compare representations, not a belief that one scale or material is always the right one.

o: A scientific ranking of living plants
Different representations of an imagined place
Practical instructions for growing plants outdoors
items.e: Mở đầu nêu paper/card/cloth và compare representations, không horticulture advice.

o: The stops on today’s guided tour
The most important works in all circumstances

items.e: Tour bắt đầu Varel directly opposite reception, không room left/right.

o: Inside the store on the right
In the discussion room on the left

items.e: One forty là giờ hiện; two ở leaflet sớm và one thirty ở wall notice cũ.

items.e: Shop bán postcards, observation desk cho mượn và nhận trả.

o: Any object if a magnifier is used

items.e: First task hướng plan, không cần modelmakingexpertise.

o: A guarantee that every visitor sees every room
A clearer way to compare representations
A rule that the most detailed model is always best
