sections.h: Listening – Part 3 · Revising a caption-design study
sections.intro: Questions 21–30. Chọn một đáp án theo cuộc thảo luận dự án học thuật tự soạn; chú ý lý do đổi thiết kế và phân công cuối.

dialog.note: Theo hai sinh viên sửa phép so phụ đề: phân yếu tố ngoài ý muốn, loại câu hỏi đo hiểu và nhiệm vụ mỗi người nhận.

lines.t: We need to explain why our assignment changed from reading speed to understanding a short recorded talk. Otherwise the tutor may think we simply forgot the original question. What should we say about the pilot?

The speed measure did not answer what interested us. People could repeat words from the captions quickly, but that did not show whether they understood the relationship between the ideas. Our pilot made us narrow the question: does a particular caption design help viewers explain the talk, rather than merely recognise its vocabulary?

That seems defensible. We are using a fictional talk about arranging a small exhibition, so we can write the script and check what information each version contains. We should say it is a classroom exercise, not a claim that our six-minute talk represents every lecture.

Yes. There are two caption versions, but I noticed a problem with the opening. In version one, the speaker introduces the three sections briefly. In version two, there is an extra explanation. If we leave it, any difference in understanding could come from the speech rather than the captions.

Then we must use the same recording for both. I had assumed that the different openings were unimportant because the main example was identical. Now I see that the introduction can guide how the later example is understood. We should remove that unintended difference before collecting more responses.

Agreed. The pilot participants also need describing accurately. They were all members of our own class, and they were comfortable with the topic vocabulary. We cannot say the group represents viewers who are new to the language or the subject. The next invitation can reach another class, but we will still have to state who actually takes part.

What should the follow-up task ask? My first draft has a list of words from the recording and asks people to define them. That might repeat the original problem of recognising vocabulary rather than following an explanation.

Let’s ask them to explain why the organiser moved the display table and what limitation remained afterwards. Those questions concern a reason and a qualification. We can still include one vocabulary check as background information, but it should not become our main measure of comprehension.

There is another detail in the captions. When the speaker says “she”, the previous visible line names two people. We know who she means from the script, but a viewer may not. Should we replace the pronoun with a name in both versions?

Yes, because an unclear reference would distract from the caption feature we intend to compare. We should record that editorial change rather than pretend the original script was always unambiguous. It also reminds us that a caption is not just a container for words; line breaks can change what information remains available at the moment a reference is read.

I’m unsure about the comment form. The tutor crossed out my question “Did the captions help you understand?” Is it wrong because it only allows yes or no, or because it suggests the result we are hoping for?

Both can limit the response, but the tutor’s main concern was the suggestion. We should begin with “Which part, if any, remained unclear?” Then we can ask what the viewer used to work it out. They might mention the spoken explanation, a diagram or the captions. We should not make captions the only explanation our question permits.

For the practical work, could you check the transcript against the recording and mark the timing of each caption? I can write the follow-up questions and organise the responses. Afterwards, we can exchange a sample to check that we have interpreted answers consistently.

I can do the transcript and timing. We also need one slide showing why we changed the design, not just a slide claiming that the final version is better. The revision is part of the reasoning: same recording, clearer reference and a task about relationships. If the results are mixed, we can still explain what the comparison shows and what another trial would need to examine. That is more convincing than announcing that captions always improve learning.

items.q: 21. Why did the project move away from reading speed?
o: Speed did not show understanding of relationships between ideas
items.e: Pilot cho repeat words nhanh nhưng chưa relationships, nên đổi measure.

items.q: 22. What unintended difference was found between versions?
o: The main example was in a different language
The screen size had already doubled
One recording had extra introductory explanation
items.e: Hai opening khác content, có thể tác động comprehension ngoài caption.

items.q: 23. What will they do about that difference?
o: Use the same recording for both versions
Keep it because introductions never matter
items.e: Họ quyết same recording, không giả rằng phần mở không ảnh hưởng.

items.q: 24. What limits the pilot group?
o: All were classmates comfortable with the vocabulary
All were entirely unfamiliar with the topic
items.e: Mẫu classmates/vocabfamiliar không đại diện mọi viewers mới môn/ngôn ngữ.

items.q: 25. Which follow-up question do they favour?
o: How quickly every word can be repeated
Which caption colour is universally best
Why the table moved and what limitation remained
items.e: Reason và qualification kiểm quan hệ ý thay vì chỉ định nghĩa từ.

items.q: 26. Why replace “she” with a name?
o: The person had changed her name
Two people were named in the preceding visible line
All pronouns are forbidden in captions
items.e: Reference ambiguity có thể gây nhiễu feature đang so, không cấm mọi pronoun.

items.q: 27. How will they treat that replacement in the report?
o: Record it as an editorial change
Pretend the first script was never ambiguous
Omit every mention of the script
items.e: Họ giữ quá trình quyết định để nguồncomparison rõ.

items.q: 28. What is the tutor’s main concern about “Did the captions help?”
o: It is impossible to answer in any form
items.e: Câu dẫn captions thành nguyên nhân mong, nên thay prompt trung tính if any unclear.

items.q: 29. What will Tavin do?
o: Check the transcript and caption timing
items.e: Cuối người thứ hai nhận transcript/timing; người đầu làm questions/responses.

items.q: 30. What should a presentation slide explain?
o: That captions always improve every learner
Only that the final file looks polished
items.e: Slide quyết định giữ reasoning/mixedresults thay tuyên universal effect.

sections.h: Listening – Part 4 · What a classroom game rewards
sections.intro: Questions 31–40. Hoàn thành ghi chú, ONE WORD ONLY. Bài giảng dùng trò chơi lớp học hư cấu để phân tích quy tắc, không công bố kết quả thực nghiệm thực tế.

dialog.note: Nghe các lần đổi luật trò chơi, ghi đúng khái niệm của từng giai đoạn và sự khác nhau giữa điều quan sát với cách diễn giải.

lines.t: In this lecture, we’ll use an invented classroom game to examine how a rule can change the activity it is supposed to organise. The Neralin Table Game was designed for groups of four. Each player had a different set of clues, and the group had to place a collection of objects on a shared plan. No player began with all the information. The resources were distributed, so cooperation was part of the task rather than an optional display of friendliness.

The first scoring rule rewarded speed. A group earned more points if it finished the plan quickly. That gave everyone a clear target, and the first trial produced several rapid arrangements. But the observers noticed that a confident player could announce a position before others had explained their clues. Some objects ended in the right place even though a player could not say why. A high score was therefore evidence of a fast result under that rule, not a complete measure of shared understanding.

The problem appeared in the explanations after the round. Two groups could show similar plans while giving very different accounts of how they reached them. One had compared the clues aloud; another had accepted a suggestion without discussing a conflicting clue. The designers did not conclude that finishing quickly was always bad. They concluded that the scoring system made explanations less visible than completion time. If understanding was an aim, the rule needed another way to preserve it.

The next version introduced rotation. Each player had one opportunity to describe a clue before the group placed an object. The order changed in the next round, so the same person did not always begin. This created space for voices that had previously been missed. It did not guarantee equal influence. A person might speak during a turn and still have their information ignored later. The report therefore distinguished an opportunity to contribute from evidence that the contribution shaped the group’s decision.

A separate observer was then added to the classroom exercise. This person did not solve the game for the players. The observer recorded which clues were discussed, when a placement changed and what remained unresolved. The role made the process available for review, but it also introduced a new condition. Players who knew they were being observed might explain more than before. The designers stated that possibility rather than treating the observer as an invisible recording device with no relation to the activity.

During discussion, players could mark an arrangement provisional. That word mattered because the group sometimes needed to place one object before another clue became available. A provisional placement was a working choice, not a final agreement. The team kept photographs of different versions of the plan so they could see why a change occurred. Without those versions, a final correct layout could conceal both a useful revision and an earlier misunderstanding.

The review also examined silence. When no one objected to a placement, the first report called the group unanimous. Interviews showed that silence could have several explanations: uncertainty, not wanting to delay others, or not yet understanding the proposal. The absence of an objection was not automatic evidence of agreement. The revised report kept the observed fact, that nobody objected at that moment, separate from the stronger interpretation of why they were silent.

Adding discussion had a cost in coordination. Rounds took longer, and the observer’s notes required time to review. More procedure was not automatically a better game. The designers wanted to know which rule helped the intended learning enough to justify the work involved. A short round followed by a focused explanation might be more useful than an elaborate system in which every action generated a record nobody examined.

The final evaluation therefore concerned decisions, not simply scores. Could players explain how a clue supported a placement? Could they revise a choice after another clue appeared? Could they identify information they still lacked? The project did not offer a universal rule for group activity. It showed how a classroom design could make its own assumptions visible, test a change and judge the result against an explicit purpose rather than the easiest number to count.

items.q: 31. Players began with different information and distributed ___ (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: Mở đầu gọi resources distributed để hợp tác thuộc cấu trúc nhiệm vụ.

items.q: 32. The first scoring rule rewarded ___ (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: First rule cho nhiều points khi finish quickly; không đo hết hiểu chung.

items.q: 33. Later ___ revealed differences behind similar final plans. (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: Đoạn ba nói explanations after round cho cách reasoning khác dù plans giống.

items.q: 34. The next version introduced ___ so each player had a turn. (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: Rotation cho mỗi người cơ hội mô tả clue và đổi người bắt đầu.

items.q: 35. A separate ___ recorded discussion without solving the game. (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: Vai observer ghi clue/change/unresolved, không đưa đáp án.

items.q: 36. A working placement could be labelled ___ (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: Provisional là lựa chọn tạm, không final agreement.

items.q: 37. Photographs preserved different ___ of the plan. (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: Giữ versions cho thấy lý do đổi và hiểu lầm sớm.

items.q: 38. Silence was not automatic evidence of ___ (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: Không objection chưa xác định tại sao im, nên không tự unanimous agreement.

items.q: 39. Added discussion had a cost in ___ (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: Đoạn gần cuối gọi cost in coordination, rounds lâu và notes cần review.

items.q: 40. Evaluation focused on ___ rather than scores alone. (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: Đoạn cuối hỏi lý do đặt, sửa khi clue mới và thông tin thiếu để xét decisions.

sections.h: Reading – Passage 1 · A wardrobe for new combinations
sections.intro: Questions 1–13. Đọc A–H, phân vật phẩm với bộ trang phục và lượt mượn với người riêng biệt. Với TRUE/FALSE/NOT GIVEN chỉ theo nguồn; câu điền theo giới hạn ghi riêng.

read.title: A wardrobe for new combinations
read.text:
A. The fictional Alverin theatre circle had collected costumes over several years, but its storage system had not grown with the collection. Boxes were labelled with the names of past productions. A new member looking for a jacket had to know which character had worn it, and a similar jacket might be hidden in a different box. The group decided to create a lending wardrobe organised for present use rather than preserve the old production boxes as the only way to find an item. The project began with a count, not with buying new clothes.

B. The inventory contained one hundred and fifty items: sixty garments, fifty accessories and forty pieces of fabric. These were not one hundred and fifty complete outfits. Some pieces could be combined in several ways, while others needed repair before use. The first inventory had only a description and a photograph. A later version added condition, location and whether an alteration could be reversed. These fields answered different questions, so a filled description did not automatically mean that an item was ready to lend.

C. The team built a simple arrangement of rails and shelves. Garments hung by item type, while accessories went into shallow trays. They considered grouping everything by a fixed character, then rejected that plan because it would make new combinations harder to imagine. Colour tags identified storage locations rather than the gender of the person who might wear an item. The catalogue kept links to earlier productions as additional information, but a borrower did not need to know those productions to find a suitable object.

D. Each member could borrow up to three items for one week. The collection opened on Sunday afternoons, and returns were due at the next Sunday opening. A group preparing a performance could request a longer period, but it had to receive confirmation before treating that request as approved. The borrowing card identified the item and the agreed return date. A verbal discussion about a possible future show did not itself reserve every costume mentioned. That distinction prevented a planning conversation from becoming a hidden claim on the wardrobe.

E. Alterations required a separate check. A borrower could fold a cuff temporarily if the fabric allowed it and the change caused no lasting mark, but could not cut or dye an item simply because it had been borrowed. A proposed permanent change went back to the wardrobe team for discussion. The rule was an agreement for this fictional collection, not a claim about all costume practice. Its purpose was to keep items usable for other members while allowing appropriate adjustments when the team understood what was proposed.

F. Volunteers received a short introduction to the catalogue. Their task was to help locate an item, record its condition and explain the agreed borrowing steps. They were not expected to tell a member that a particular appearance was correct for a role or to invent a history for an unlabelled object. If a photograph was unclear, the volunteer could ask for a new one at the next inventory session. The record should reflect what was known, rather than become more confident simply because a visitor had asked a question.

G. During the first month, twenty-four loans were recorded. This was a count of borrowing transactions, not necessarily of twenty-four different people. Some members borrowed on more than one Sunday. Several comments praised how quickly a garment could be found, but the group did not compare search time with the old system under identical conditions. It therefore reported a positive response rather than a measured reduction of a particular number of minutes. The new catalogue made a more detailed future comparison possible by recording the location searched and the item requested.

H. The project also changed what members noticed about the collection. Fabric once treated as leftovers could be considered for a new scene, and accessories could move between productions. The team planned a small display showing two different uses of selected items, with permission from those involved in the examples. It would not imply that every object had been fully documented. The wardrobe remained a working resource, and its usefulness depended on regular checking, clear agreements and space for combinations that the original storage labels had not anticipated.

sections.h: Reading – Passage 2 · A label does more than name
sections.intro: Questions 14–26. Chọn heading theo chức năng đoạn, phân TRUE/FALSE/NOT GIVEN theo nội dung và điền ONE WORD ONLY. Mọi nhãn, nguồn và triển lãm là ví dụ tự soạn.

read.title: A label does more than name
read.text:
A. A translated label can contain familiar words and still direct attention differently from its source. The problem is not always an inaccurate dictionary choice. A label has a purpose, a position and a reader, and these conditions help determine what its sentence does. A phrase intended to invite reflection can become a command about behaviour; a statement of possibility can become a claim of fact. Translating a public display therefore requires attention to relationships that extend beyond matching one word with another.

B. The fictional Torelan exhibition tested two English versions of a short source note. The note was described as an invitation to pause before making a choice. One version called the object “a waiting area”. Another called it “a place to pause before choosing”. The first was shorter, but it suggested a practical function that the source had not assigned. Visitors might reasonably look for somewhere to wait rather than consider a decision. The difference was small in word count and substantial in the role offered to the reader.

C. The team did not conclude that longer labels were always more faithful. Another sentence contained a specialised term followed by three explanations. The revised version kept the central relationship and moved an additional explanation to an optional guide. Readers who wanted it could investigate further without every visitor having to process the same amount of text. The guide could also show why an unusual expression mattered. The report made no claim about what all children or all adults prefer. It described a design choice for this exhibition and the information each part of the display was meant to provide.

D. Position created a different difficulty. The source used a word equivalent to “here”, but the translated label was to be moved from a wall to a portable guide. If the word were retained without checking its reference, readers could attach it to wherever they happened to stand. The translator therefore needed to ask whether “here” meant beside the object, within the imagined scene or at this stage of the story. Changing the location of a text could change its reference even when every word remained grammatically correct.

E. Qualifications required equal care. An archive note said that an object might have been used in a particular activity. A draft translation described the use as established. That made the sentence more direct but removed an uncertainty present in the source. The team restored the qualification and explained that the evidence was incomplete. Simplicity did not justify exchanging a possible history for a confirmed one. The reader needed access to the uncertainty because it affected what could reasonably be concluded about the object.

F. The review included a separate factual pass. Reviewers compared numbers, names and relations between dates across versions. This was not a glamorous stage, but it could catch a shift that fluent prose concealed. In one invented example, a list counted parts of an object while the label called them separate objects. The words were individually plausible; the unit had changed. The team recorded that correction rather than treat accuracy as a single impression formed after reading the final paragraph aloud.

G. Reviewers also disagreed about tone. One wanted the label to preserve the artist’s unusual phrasing; another wanted a first-time visitor to understand the invitation without additional explanation. Neither aim could be settled by counting words alone. The group asked what would be lost if a phrase changed and whether the display could retain the unusual expression while providing a short clarification. The resulting choice was not neutral, but the reasons were visible. A record of disagreement helped later reviewers understand why an apparently obvious alternative had not been selected.

H. The project saved the source description, the two drafts and the reasons for revision. It did not keep every minor adjustment as a separate public document, but it preserved the choices that changed interpretation. A final label could then be read as the outcome of an accountable process rather than as a transparent window onto one fixed meaning. Translation remained an act of judgement. Its quality depended on preserving what the source warranted, explaining essential references and giving the intended reader a workable route into the display without quietly inventing a different message.

sections.h: Reading – Passage 3 · What a team credit leaves unsaid
sections.intro: Questions 27–40. Các vai trong dự án hư cấu có thể chồng nhau, không cộng thành số người nếu nguồn nói cùng nhóm. YES/NO/NOT GIVEN theo quan điểm và nội dung bài; câu điền ONE WORD ONLY.

read.title: What a team credit leaves unsaid
read.text:
A. The phrase “a team achievement” can recognise cooperation, but it can also make the team appear as one actor with one intention. A finished book or exhibition rarely displays the distribution of work that made it possible. Some decisions remain visible in the object, while scheduling, checking and explaining may leave a less obvious trace. Deciding how to acknowledge a collective project therefore involves more than finding a short phrase that sounds generous. It requires an account of which contributions matter to the purpose of the acknowledgement.

B. Consider an invented story collection made by the Ravelin writing circle. Twelve people contributed texts. Six of those same contributors also edited, and two also worked on layout. These were overlapping roles, not twenty separate participants. A first public description named the coordinator as the person who “created the collection”. The coordinator had arranged meetings and brought the files together, but the phrase could imply authorship of the texts and decisions made by others. The group needed to revise the account without pretending that coordination had been irrelevant.

C. An early correction swung towards another simplification. It described all twelve people as having contributed equally in every role. That was not what the working record showed. Different members had written different amounts, checked different sections and participated at different stages. Equal respect did not require an invented equality of tasks. The group could acknowledge each person’s contribution while making the categories clear, rather than treating fairness as a reason to erase every difference in what had occurred.

D. The record itself was not complete. Editing logs showed changes to sentences, but not every conversation that led to them. A member who suggested a question during a meeting might have influenced an ending without touching the file. Conversely, a name attached to many small corrections did not necessarily identify the person responsible for the main interpretation. The group compared saved versions with meeting notes and short accounts from participants. Each source could illuminate a different part of the work, and each needed to be examined rather than accepted as a transparent measure of contribution.

E. There was also a temporal problem. After seeing the successful collection, participants could describe an uncertain experiment as though the plan had been clear from the start. The review tried to preserve changes of mind. An abandoned structure could show useful reasoning even if it left no direct trace in the final pages. This did not mean that every rejected suggestion deserved the same prominence as a completed text. It meant that the acknowledgement should not be built entirely from what happened to remain visible at the end.

F. Less visible work required explicit attention. Someone had arranged a quiet meeting place; another had checked that the printed copies matched the approved file. These tasks enabled the work without becoming its main content. Whether they belonged in a brief label or a longer process note depended partly on the purpose of the document. A reading invitation might need author names and an event contact, while a teaching account could explain the steps through which the collection developed. No single list could do all these jobs equally well.

G. The question used to gather evidence mattered too. “Who deserves the most credit?” assumed that the aim was to rank everyone on one scale. The group instead asked which decisions a person had made, what work they had carried out and which other contributions had enabled it. Those questions did not eliminate judgement. They made it more specific. The resulting account could show cooperation without converting a complex process into a contest whose rules had never been discussed.

H. Shared authorship also did not remove individual responsibility. If a passage contained an error, the group still needed a route for checking and correcting it. Naming roles helped readers know whom to contact, but the group avoided treating the person who handled the final file as automatically responsible for every earlier choice. Accountability required a record of decisions and an agreed way to revise the publication. Distributing credit and locating responsibility were related questions, not exact mirror images of one another.

I. The final description used layered acknowledgement: a concise public list with clearly named roles and a separate note about the process. Participants checked how their work was described and could ask for a correction. The account was not mathematically exact, because unlike tasks had not been converted into a single unit. It was more defensible because its distinctions and purpose were open. A fair acknowledgement is an argument about contribution, supported by a record and a revisable procedure; it is not a flattering phrase that makes the history of collaboration unnecessary to examine.

sections.intro: Khoảng 20 phút. Biểu đồ tự soạn gồm hai tổng riêng đều bằng 100%; tối thiểu 150 từ.

write.task: The bar chart compares the percentage of project time that two fictional groups allocated to planning, making and review. Summarise the main features and make relevant comparisons. Write at least 150 words. Không có tổng thời gian theo giờ; không tự đổi phần trăm thành số phút.

chart.title: Distribution of project time in two fictional groups

write.model: The bar chart compares how two fictional groups divided their project time between planning, making and review. Overall, making accounted for the largest share in both groups. Group A devoted a greater proportion to planning, whereas Group B allocated more time proportionally to review and slightly more to making. For Group A, planning represented forty per cent of the total. Making was only five percentage points higher, at forty-five per cent, while review took the remaining fifteen per cent. The distribution was therefore weighted towards the first two stages, which together accounted for eighty-five per cent. Group B spent half of its project time on making. Planning and review each represented one quarter, so these two stages were equal within that group. Compared with Group A, its planning share was fifteen percentage points lower and its review share ten points higher. Its making share exceeded Group A’s by five points. The figures describe proportions of each group’s total rather than a common number of hours. Consequently, they do not establish which group spent more actual time on any stage or completed the project faster.
write.modelVi: Biểu đồ so cách hai nhóm giả chia thời gian cho lập kế hoạch, làm và review. Cả hai dành nhiều nhất cho làm. A có phần kế hoạch cao hơn, B có phần review cao hơn và làm nhỉnh hơn. A dành bốn mươi phần trăm kế hoạch, bốn mươi lăm làm, mười lăm review, nên hai bước đầu cộng tám mươi lăm. B dành nửa cho làm, hai bước còn lại mỗi một phần tư. So A, B kế hoạch thấp mười lăm điểm, review cao mười và làm cao năm. Đây là tỉ trọng tổng riêng, chưa tổng giờ chung, nên không xác định ai dành số giờ thật nhiều hơn hoặc xong nhanh hơn.
rubric: Task achievement: overview và so sánh chính đúng số, tối thiểu 150 từ.
Coherence and cohesion: nhóm theo phân bố và đối chiếu, không nhầm trình tự thời gian với thay đổi theo năm.
Lexical resource: phân biệt proportion, actual time và percentage points.
Grammatical range and accuracy: câu so sánh/mệnh đề hạn chế có kiểm soát, không thêm nguyên nhân ngoài biểu đồ.

sections.intro: Khoảng 40 phút. Thảo luận hai quan điểm về đối tượng triển lãm rồi nêu ý riêng; tối thiểu 250 từ.

write.task: Some people think public exhibitions should be designed mainly for experts, while others believe they should focus on people with little previous knowledge. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words. Give reasons and relevant examples.
write.model: Public exhibitions need not choose between depth and accessibility as though one necessarily excludes the other. Although expert visitors deserve material that rewards their knowledge, I believe the main route through a public exhibition should be understandable without specialist preparation, with optional opportunities for further investigation. Those who prioritise experts can argue that a display loses value if difficult ideas are simplified until their important distinctions disappear. A specialised comparison may require vocabulary and background that a short label cannot supply. For a visitor who has studied the subject, repeating only introductory information can make an exhibition feel superficial. This is a legitimate concern, and advanced material should have a place. However, a public exhibition also invites people who have not yet acquired that background. If the first label assumes an unexplained technical system, a newcomer may be unable to ask a useful question or recognise what is worth examining. In an imagined display of paper models, a clear account of the main design choice could allow a first-time visitor to compare two versions, even without knowing specialist terminology. That opening does not require the curator to claim that the explanation is complete. I would therefore use a layered design. The main display would establish the purpose, essential references and a few revealing comparisons. A separate guide or optional section could provide detailed debate, sources and technical language for interested visitors, including newcomers who want to continue. Organisers should test whether both routes work rather than count only the comments of the most confident visitors. Such an arrangement gives priority to entry without treating learning as a fixed divide between experts and everyone else. It allows the exhibition to welcome a reader and still offer somewhere further to go.
write.modelVi: Triển lãm không cần chọn sâu hoặc tiếp cận như loại trừ nhau. Tôi cho lối chính nên hiểu không cần nền chuyên môn, kèm tùy chọn tìm sâu. Người ưu tiên chuyên gia có lý: đơn giản quá có thể mất phân biệt, so chuyên sâu cần thuật ngữ/nền hơn nhãn ngắn; chỉ nhập môn làm người đã học thấy hời hợt. Nhưng công chúng gồm người chưa có nền: nhãn đầu giả định hệ kỹ thuật không giải thích khiến họ khó hỏi hoặc thấy cần xem gì. Ví dụ giả mô hình giấy, mô tả lựa chọn chính cho khách mới so hai bản không cần thuật ngữ, không tự nhận đầy đủ. Tôi chọn nhiều lớp: phần chính có mục đích, tham chiếu cần và vài phép so; guide riêng có tranh luận, nguồn, kỹ thuật cho người muốn sâu kể cả người mới. Cần thử hai lối với người đa dạng, không chỉ tự tin nhất. Ưu tiên cửa vào không chia cố định chuyên gia/người khác, vừa chào đón vừa có bước tiếp.
rubric: Task response: tối thiểu 250 từ, lý do cả hai views và lập trường riêng rõ.
Coherence and cohesion: luận điểm, ví dụ và phản biện nối với cách thiết kế được đề xuất.
Lexical resource: ngôn ngữ audience, depth, accessibility đúng nghĩa, ví dụ được nêu hư cấu.
Grammatical range and accuracy: phối cấu trúc nhượng bộ, điều kiện và so sánh chính xác; không cố từ hiếm làm mờ ý.

sections.intro: Người hỏi chọn câu về hợp tác, góp ý và hình ảnh; hỏi tiếp theo phản hồi thực.

tasks.p: Do you like working with other people?
tasks.model: Usually, yes, when the purpose and responsibilities are clear. Another person can notice a problem I have missed. I find it harder when everyone assumes that someone else will make the final decision.

tasks.p: What do you usually do when a group disagrees?
tasks.model: I first try to check whether we are answering the same question. Sometimes one person is thinking about speed while another is thinking about detail. Naming the criteria can make the disagreement easier to discuss.

tasks.p: Have you ever learned from someone’s suggestion?
tasks.model: Yes. A useful suggestion is often quite specific, such as asking whether a reader can identify the person named by a pronoun. That gives me something to test rather than a general instruction to make the work better.

tasks.p: Did you enjoy drawing when you were younger?
tasks.model: I enjoyed quick sketches more than carefully finished pictures. I liked trying a shape in several ways. These days I still draw small diagrams when I need to explain a position or a sequence.

tasks.p: Do you prefer looking at a picture or reading its explanation first?
tasks.model: I usually look first, then read if I want more context. An explanation can direct my attention to something I missed, but I also like a moment to form my own question.

tasks.p: Would you keep an early draft of something you made?
tasks.model: I would keep a few versions if they show an important change. I do not need every tiny adjustment, but a selected draft can help me remember why I chose the final arrangement.

rubric: Đáp liên quan với thói quen, ý kiến hoặc trải nghiệm thật của người học.
Phát triển vừa đủ bằng lý do cụ thể, không kéo thành bài luận thuộc.
Nghe lại để kiểm câu hỏi nào đã được đáp và chỗ âm/nhịp gây khó hiểu.

sections.intro: Thẻ nói dài về thay đổi kế hoạch sau góp ý; dùng từ khóa chuẩn bị và triển khai tự nhiên.

tasks.p: Describe a plan that changed after someone made a suggestion. You should say what the plan was, who made the suggestion, what changed, and explain why the change mattered. Chuẩn bị một phút, nói một đến hai phút; nếu luyện bằng trường hợp giả, hãy nói rõ.
tasks.model: For this practice, I’ll use an invented example from a small story display. The original plan was to put a long explanation beside every picture, because the organisers wanted visitors to understand all the background. A volunteer who was new to the project tried following the route and said that she kept reading without having enough time to look. She did not ask them to remove the information completely. Her suggestion was to keep a short question beside each picture and put the longer explanations in an optional guide. The team tested that arrangement with two pictures before changing the whole room. It created more space around the images and allowed a visitor to decide when to read further. The organisers still had to check whether the short questions made sense without the extra text. I would choose this example because the suggestion changed the role of the explanation rather than merely reducing its length. It also came from someone who did not share all the background knowledge of the team. The change mattered because the display was meant to welcome first-time visitors, not only confirm what its makers already understood. It was a limited test, so the team kept a review date instead of claiming that the new layout would suit every exhibition.

rubric: Theo đủ bốn gợi ý và phát triển chuỗi kế hoạch–góp ý–thử–ý nghĩa.
Phân biệt điều thật đã đổi với hiệu quả còn cần kiểm; chuyện thật của người học không cần giống mẫu.
Thử thời lượng khi nói, giữ nhịp và âm cuối, không đọc nguyên bản như trải nghiệm thật.

sections.intro: Thảo luận từ góp ý sang chuyên môn, đồng thuận và hồ sơ dự án; có thể thêm phản ví dụ liên quan.

tasks.p: Why can an outsider sometimes give useful advice?
tasks.model: An outsider may notice an assumption that the group no longer sees because it has become familiar. In a display, for example, the makers may understand a label only because they already know the story. A new visitor can reveal that gap. However, being outside does not automatically make someone right. I would treat the comment as a reason to examine the design, not as a complete replacement for the group’s knowledge.

tasks.p: Should a group always reach agreement before acting?
tasks.model: It depends on the decision and whether it can be revised. Some choices need everyone’s consent because they affect each person directly. Others can proceed as a limited trial while disagreement is recorded. What I would avoid is manufacturing agreement by treating silence as acceptance. The group should explain who decides, what concerns remain and what would make the choice change later.

tasks.p: Is it important to keep records of how a project developed?
tasks.model: Selected records can help people understand why a choice was made and prevent a later account from making the process seem more straightforward than it was. But keeping every file is not the same as making a usable record. Versions need dates, relationships and an explanation of important changes. I would preserve material that helps answer a defined question, while respecting any limits on sharing it.

tasks.p: How can organisers include both experts and newcomers in a discussion?
tasks.model: They can establish the main question in ordinary language without pretending that the subject has no complexity. Experts can then explain a distinction through an example, and newcomers can ask about assumptions rather than be expected to know all the terminology. It also helps to provide more than one way to respond. A written comment after the meeting may reveal a concern that was not easy to express during a fast discussion.

rubric: Có khái quát với lý do và giới hạn, phản hồi được câu hỏi tiếp.
Nguồn từ và ngữ pháp nâng cao phục vụ ý, không biến một ví dụ thành quy tắc mọi nơi.
Đánh giá thể hiện theo mạch lạc, từ, ngữ pháp và phát âm, không đưa điểm chứng chỉ tự động.
